title: Software Extensions: Browser Extensions
summary: Browser extensions are small programs loaded into the browser itself, and they are the most common member of the software extension family because they follow the browser everywhere, including onto personal and unmanaged machines. What makes the sub-technique distinct is the reach of the host: an extension added to a browser profile can read and modify pages the user visits, reach stored cookies and saved form data, observe downloads and, with the right permission, talk to any address on the network the browser can reach. Installation has several routes. The ordinary one is the vendor marketplace, where a malicious listing can impersonate a popular extension, buy its way up the recommendation list, or arrive through a legitimate extension that was sold or hijacked and then updated with new code. The quieter route does not involve the user at all: while the browser is closed, an attacker with local access edits the profile configuration files that record installed extensions and their permissions, so the extension loads from disk at the next start with no prompt and no marketplace review. Management policy can also be used, and on managed fleets both enterprise policy and platform configuration profiles are legitimate tools that an attacker can imitate. Detection therefore starts with visibility into the browser profile, which means reading the extension folder and the policy settings rather than relying on a visual check of the toolbar, and comparing what is installed with what the marketplace or change records show. Malicious extensions blend very well into ordinary browsing, so the stronger signals are extensions that were added without a user prompt, extensions whose update address points outside the official store, and browsing sessions that produce authentication or download activity the user does not remember.

beginner.definition: A browser extension is an add-on that changes how your web browser works, for example a password helper or an ad blocker. This technique is when an attacker uses such an add-on to keep access to your accounts and your browsing.
beginner.whyItMatters: The extension runs inside your browser, so it can see pages, cookies and saved logins. An attacker can hide one in the browser profile, and it will load without asking you. Because extensions are normal, a strange one is easy to miss for a long time.
howItWorks: Browsers load extensions from a special extension folder inside your user profile.
A profile file records each extension, together with its version and its permissions.
Attackers can publish a fake extension in the store, hoping you install it.
They can also edit those profile files while the browser is closed.
The next time the browser starts, the extension loads silently in the background.
It can then read pages, take cookies or send data to the attacker.
beginner.example: Imagine a hotel where guests may hire a porter from the lobby desk. One porter is listed on the official board but also carries a key to every room on the floor. Each time a guest unlocks their door, the porter quietly notes what is inside. The desk never checks the porter again after hiring.
takeaways: Extensions share the browser permissions, so they are not cut off from your data.
Check the extension folder and the browser policy, not just the toolbar.
An extension installed with no user prompt should be treated as suspicious.

objectives: Explain how a browser extension is installed and where its settings live.
Describe how this sub-technique differs from the parent technique Software Extensions.
Describe how a browser profile can be edited to load an extension without consent.
Identify the extension metadata, policy settings and store records that reveal an addition.
Explain why an extension can read cookies and pages the user visits.
